sketches.title: Tide Turners
sketches.premise: The sea and the shore take turns sending forces against each other. Name one standing sea-or-shore thing that defeats the thing just played, then explain the clash in one vivid sentence.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts a move only when the new thing directly blocks, breaks, drains, buries, erodes, traps, or otherwise overcomes what stands; dodging, merely surviving, hiding, and a bigger or louder copy lose.
sketches.move_shape: Say “I am [thing], [action] [standing thing].” Example: “I am a seawall, stopping the wave in a thunderous slap.” The host declares, “The wave has met architecture—and lost its dramatic entrance.”
sketches.first_card: I am a wave, rolling toward the shore.

sketches.title: Shoreline Stack
sketches.premise: Build one impossible shoreline by placing sea and shore objects in a chain. Each turn adds a standing thing that uses the last thing as a material, support, or obstacle, so the beach grows stranger while still making plain sense.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts an addition only if it directly acts on the last object by holding, covering, carrying, shaping, filling, or stopping it; a thing that merely sits beside it, resembles it, or is a larger version loses.
sketches.move_shape: Say “I add [thing], which [clear action] [last thing].” Example: “I add sand, filling the shell.” The host proclaims, “The shell has been promoted to a sandcastle’s foundation, a noble but dusty career.”
sketches.first_card: A shell lies on wet sand.

sketches.title: Wreck and Rescue
sketches.premise: A storm has scattered a shipwreck along the coast. One player names a sea danger or problem; the other names an everyday sea-or-shore tool, creature, or force that fixes that exact problem, then the roles switch.
sketches.criterion: A rescue counts only when it directly removes, repairs, carries, reveals, or safely contains the stated problem; merely avoiding danger, enduring it, or choosing a stronger version of it loses.
sketches.move_shape: The danger is stated, then answer: “I send [thing], which [action] the problem.” Example: “I send a rope, pulling the boat from the rocks.” The host announces, “At last, a rope with a plan instead of a wet piece of string.”
sketches.first_card: A wave smashes a small boat onto rocks.

sketches.title: Beach Battle Plans
sketches.premise: Two rival captains command tiny fleets made from things found at the sea and shore. On each turn, play one piece to capture the opponent’s last piece by using a plain weakness, tool, or natural force.
sketches.criterion: A capture is valid only when the new piece directly makes the last piece unable to act, stay, or escape; a piece that merely outruns it, hides from it, or is a bigger member of its family loses.
sketches.move_shape: Say “My [piece] captures your [piece] because it [direct action].” Example: “My net captures your fish because it tangles its fins.” The host cries, “The fish has discovered that freedom is not guaranteed by having fins.”
sketches.first_card: My wave is the first piece on the board.

sketches.title: Salt Sandwich
sketches.premise: Make a chain of sea-and-shore things where every new thing changes the taste, shape, or use of the one before it. The chain must stay concrete: each move is a thing doing something to its predecessor.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts a move only when the new thing directly dissolves, coats, stains, hardens, softens, mixes with, or reshapes the standing thing; a metaphor with no working mechanism, a dodge, and a stronger copy lose.
sketches.move_shape: Say “I am [thing], and I [action] the [standing thing].” Example: “I am salt, and I season the shellfish.” The host declares, “The shellfish has been seasoned by destiny—or at least by lunch.”
sketches.first_card: I am seawater, salty and splashing.

sketches.title: Lighthouse Last Word
sketches.premise: The coast is a stage, and every turn sends one clear signal or force against the last one. Keep answering with something from sea or shore that can plainly stop, reveal, redirect, or transform what stands until one answer fails.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts only a direct overcoming action—blocking, revealing, redirecting, grounding, drying, freezing, or transforming the standing thing; surviving, sidestepping, hiding, and saying “a bigger one” are losses.
sketches.move_shape: Say “I am [thing], [action] [standing thing].” Example: “I am fog, hiding the lighthouse beam.” The host booms, “The lighthouse has been defeated by weather’s least impressive curtain.”
sketches.first_card: I am a lighthouse beam, sweeping across the dark water.
